¶
'''unheroic''' (un-hẹ̄-rō′ik), ''a.'' Not heroic.

'''unheroism''' (un-her′ọ̄-izm), ''n.'' That which is not heroic; unheroic character or action; cowardice. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Their greedy quackeries and ''unheroisms.''
{{right|''Carlyle'', Cromwell, i. 65.}}}}

'''unhesitating''' (un-hes′i-tā-ting), ''a.'' Not hesitating; without misgiving or doubt; prompt; ready.

'''unhesitatingly''' (un-hes′i-tā-ting-li), ''adv.'' Without hesitation or doubt.

'''unhidden''' (un-hid′n), ''a.'' Not hidden or concealed; open; manifest. ''Shak.'', Hen. V., i. 1. 86.

'''unhide†''' (un-hīd′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unhiden''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''hide''<sup>1</sup>.] To reveal the nature of; disclose.
{{smaller block|Tyl I this romance may ''unhide.''
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 2168.}}}}

'''unhill†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''unhillen'', ''unhilen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''hill''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''unheal''<sup>2</sup>.] To uncover; unroof.
{{smaller block|<poem>And if his hous be ''vnhiled'' and reyne on his bedde,
He seketh and seketh til he slepe drye.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xvii. 319.}}}}

'''unhinge''' (un-hinj′), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To take from the hinges: as, to ''unhinge'' a door.
{{smaller block|<poem>Paul’s midnight voice prevail’d, his music’s thunder
''Unhing’d'' the prison-doors, split bolts in sunder.</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, v., Epig. 10.}}}}
'''2.''' To displace; unfix by violence.
{{smaller block|<poem>Rather than not accomplish my revenge,
Just or unjust, I would the world ''unhinge.'' ''Waller.''</poem>}}
'''3.''' To unsettle; loosen; render unstable or wavering; discompose; disorder: as, to ''unhinge''
readings.c1s3:
the mind; to ''unhinge'' opinions.
{{smaller block|Wingy mysteries in divinity, and airy subtleties in religion, which have ''unhinged'' the brains of better heads.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Religio Medici, i. 9.}}}}

'''unhingement''' (un-hinj′mẹnt), ''n.'' The act of unhinging, or the state of being unhinged. ''Imp. Dict.'' [Rare.]

'''unhired''' (un-hīrd′), ''a.'' Not hired. ''Milton'', Touching Hirelings.

'''unhistoric''' (un-his-tor′ik), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not historic; not containing or conveying history; not being a part of recorded history; not noticed in history; unrecorded.
{{smaller block|Through how many ages this ''unhistoric'' night of European man may have preceded the dawn of civilisation it is at present vain to speculate.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', II. 342.}}}}
'''2.''' Contrary to history. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Under the influence of crude and ''unhistoric'' discussion of the subject . . . this conception of the American state has passed from the minds of large bodies of our people.
{{right|''Bibliotheca Sacra'', XLVI. 545.}}
Of Disraeli, in 1874, there is an equally speculative and ''unhistoric'' judgment. ''The Academy'', Dec. 27, 1890, p. 606.}}

'''unhistorical''' (un-his-tor′i-kạl), ''a.'' Same as ''unhistoric''.

'''unhitch''' (un-hich′), ''v. t.'' To disengage from a hitch or fastening; set free; unfasten: as, to ''unhitch'' a horse.

'''unhive''' (un-hīv′), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To drive from a hive. —'''2.''' To deprive of habitation or shelter.
readings.c3s1:
{{smaller block|<poem>Maidens wave
Their kerchiefs, and old women weep for joy;
While others, not so satisfied, ''unhorse''
The gilded equipage, and, turning loose
His steeds, usurp a place they well deserve.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, vi. 701.}}}}

'''unhospitable''' (un-hos′pi-ta̤-bl), ''a.'' Inhospitable. [Rare.]

'''unhospital†''' (un-hos′pi-ta̤l), ''a.'' Inhospitable. ''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 39.

'''unhostile''' (un-hos′til), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not hostile; friendly.—'''2.''' Not pertaining to or caused by an enemy. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|By ''unhostile'' wounds destroy’d. ''J. Philips'', Blenheim.}}

'''unhouse''' (un-houz′), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To drive from the house or habitation; dislodge. ''Milton'', On the Death of a Fair Infant, l. 21.—'''2.''' To deprive of shelter. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''unhoused''' (un-houzd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not housed or sheltered as by a house; having no house or home. ''Whittier'', Tent on the Beach.—'''2.''' Deprived of or driven from a house, home, roof, or shelter. ''Shak.'', T. of A., iv. 3. 229.

'''unhouseled†''', '''unhouselled†''' (un-hou′zeld), ''a.'' Not having received the sacrament.
{{smaller block|<poem>Cut off even in the blossom of my sin,
''Unhousel’d'', disappointed, unaneled.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 5. 77.}}}}

'''unhuman''' (un-hū′man), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not human; destitute of human qualities. ''R. L. Stevenson'', Thoreau, IV.—'''2.''' Inhuman. [Rare.]

¶
'''unhusbanding†''' (un-huz′ban-ding), ''n.'' [ME. ''unhusbondyng''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''husbanding''.] Neglect to till; failure to cultivate. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>In housbonding is mysse,
''Unhusbondyng'' undooth fertilitee.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius,'' Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 11.}}}}

'''unhusk''' (un-husk′), ''v. t.'' To deprive of a husk, as corn; hence, figuratively, to cause (a person) to reveal his thoughts or purposes; cause to disclose.
{{smaller block|<poem>The Duke’s sonne warily enquir’d for me,
Whose pleasure I attended; he began
By policy to open and ''unhuske'' me
About the time and common rumour.</poem>
{{right|''C. Tourneur,'' Revenger’s Tragedy, i. 1.}}}}

'''uniarticulate''' (ū″ni-är-tik′ū-lāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus,'' one (= E. ''one''), + ''articulus,'' joint: see ''articulate''.] Having but one joint; single-jointed: opposed to ''bi-'', ''tri-'', or ''multi-articulate''.

'''Uniat, Uniate''' (ū′ni-at, -āt), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< Russ. ''uniyatŭ,'' a united Greek, < L. ''unus,'' one: see ''unite''.] '''I.''' ''n.'' A member of one of those communities which have separated from one of the Oriental churches and submitted to the supremacy of the Pope, and to the doctrinal decisions of the Roman Church, while retaining their ancient liturgy, rites, discipline, or other of their distinctive usages to a greater or less extent, but with some important modifications; specifically, one of the United Greeks. See ''united''.
